content: In Georgia, cases of dermatophytosis caused by Trichophyton species and Microsporum gypseum were documented among individuals and families who exhibited lambs. In 1986, an outbreak of ringworm affecting 23 people and multiple animal species was traced to a Microsporum canis infection in a hand-reared zoo tiger cub. Infections with the orf virus, also known as contagious ecthyma or sore mouth in sheep and goats, have occurred following contact with sheep in public settings. Orf virus infections have also been reported in goats and sheep at children’s petting zoos and in lambs used for Easter photo opportunities. Transmission of poxviruses in public settings has been documented. For example, in the 1970s, a zoo attendant developed an extensive papular skin rash caused by a cowpox-like virus after handling various species of infected exotic animals. Cowpox virus transmission from rats to humans has been reported among individuals who purchased rats as pets or had contact with them in pet stores. In 2003, multiple cases of monkeypox occurred among individuals who had contact with infected prairie dogs, either at a child-care center or a pet store. Aquatic animals and their environments have been associated with cutaneous infections. For instance, Mycobacterium marinum infections have been reported among individuals who own or clean fish tanks. Ectoparasites and endoparasites present risks when humans interact with exhibit animals. Sarcoptes scabiei, a skin mite, can infest humans and animals, including swine, dogs, cats, foxes, cattle, and coyotes. Although human infestations from animal sources are usually self-limiting, they can cause skin irritation and itching for several days and may be challenging to diagnose. Bites from avian mites have been reported in association with pet gerbils in school settings. Fleas from animals that bite humans can increase the risk of infection or allergic reactions. Additionally, fleas can carry a tapeworm species that may infect children who accidentally ingest the flea. Animal parasites can also infect humans who ingest materials contaminated with animal feces or come into contact with contaminated soil. Parasite control through veterinary care, proper husbandry, and handwashing reduces the risks associated with ectoparasites and endoparasites. Tuberculosis is another disease of concern in certain animal settings. In 1996, 12 circus elephant handlers at an exotic animal farm in Illinois were infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis. One handler exhibited signs consistent with active disease after three elephants died of tuberculosis. Between 1989 and 1991, at a zoo in Louisiana, seven animal handlers who were previously negative for tuberculosis tested positive following a Mycobacterium bovis outbreak in rhinoceroses and monkeys. Other instances of transmission of mycobacterial species from animals to animal care staff, without known transmission to the public, have also been documented. The U.S. Zoonotic pathogens can also be transmitted through direct or indirect contact with reproductive fluids, aborted fetuses, or newborns from infected dams. Live-birthing exhibits, often involving livestock such as cattle, pigs, goats, or sheep, are popular at agricultural fairs. Although the public typically does not have direct contact with animals during birthing, newborns and their dams may be available for petting afterward. Serious zoonoses, such as Q fever (Coxiella burnetii), leptospirosis, listeriosis, brucellosis, and chlamydiosis, can be acquired through contact with reproductive materials. C. burnetii is a rickettsial organism that most frequently infects cattle, sheep, and goats. The disease can cause abortion in animals but is more often asymptomatic. During birthing, infected animals shed large numbers of organisms, which can become aerosolized. Most individuals exposed to C. burnetii develop asymptomatic infections, but clinical illness can range from an acute influenza-like illness to life-threatening endocarditis. A Q fever outbreak involving 95 confirmed cases and 41 hospitalizations was linked to goats and sheep giving birth at petting zoos in indoor shopping malls. Indoor birthing exhibits may pose an increased risk for Q fever transmission due to inadequate ventilation. Chlamydophila psittaci infections, which cause respiratory disease, are usually acquired from psittacine birds. For example, an outbreak of C. psittaci pneumonia occurred among staff members at the Copenhagen Zoological Garden. On rare occasions, chlamydial infections acquired from sheep, goats, and birds have resulted in reproductive problems in women. Transmission of influenza viruses between humans and animals has implications for animals in public settings. Cases and clusters of human infection with swine influenza viruses have been sporadically reported since the 1970s, with several cases linked to swine at agricultural fairs. Conversely, transmission of human influenza viruses to swine has also been documented. For instance, in 2009, an H1N1 influenza virus strain emerged, causing a pandemic among humans with sporadic transmission from humans to swine. Guidelines from multiple organizations were used to create the recommendations in this report. Although no federal U.S. laws specifically address the risk of pathogen transmission at venues where the public has contact with animals, some states have enacted such laws. For example, in 2005, North Carolina enacted legislation requiring individuals displaying animals for public contact at agricultural fairs to obtain a permit from the North Carolina Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services. Certain federal agencies and associations in the United States have developed standards, recommendations, and guidelines for reducing risks associated with public contact with animals in zoologic parks. The Association of Zoos and Aquariums has accreditation standards for minimizing the risk of animal contact with the public in zoologic parks. In accordance with the Animal Welfare Act, the USDA licenses and inspects certain animal exhibits. These inspections primarily address humane treatment but also impact the health of the animals and the safety of the public. In 2001, the CDC issued guidelines to reduce the risk of infection with enteric pathogens associated with farm visits. The CDC has also issued recommendations for preventing the transmission of Salmonella from reptiles, amphibians, and live poultry to humans. The Association for Professionals in Infection Control and Epidemiology (APIC) and the Animal-Assisted Interventions Working Group (AAI) have developed guidelines to address risks associated with the use of animals in healthcare settings.
